details:
**Pygmalion**
Shaw's most famous play (1913), named after the Greek myth of the sculptor whose statue comes to life. The phonetics professor Henry Higgins bets Colonel Pickering that he can teach the Cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle to speak so well that she could pass for a duchess. It opens outside Covent Garden, where Higgins, at first called "the note-taker," is copying down Eliza's speech and she fears he is a police informer. It was later adapted as the musical My Fair Lady.

**"Walk! Not bloody likely!"**
Eliza's shocking exit line in Act III of Pygmalion, when Freddy offers to walk her across the park after Mrs. Higgins's at-home. During the same visit she describes how her gin-loving aunt was "done in," and Freddy's sister Clara calls it "the new small talk," which she finds "delightful and quite innocent." Shaw's friend Mrs. Patrick Campbell spoke the line in the first London production, scandalizing audiences.

**Freddy Eynsford-Hill and "What Happened Afterwards"**
Freddy is the poor young gentleman who bumps into Eliza at Covent Garden, making her drop her flowers, and later falls in love with her. Annoyed by actor-manager Herbert Beerbohm Tree's attempts to give the play a romantic ending with Higgins, Shaw added a prose sequel, "What Happened Afterwards," explaining that Eliza marries Freddy and they open a flower shop.

**Eliza's rebellion and Alfred Doolittle**
At the end of Pygmalion, after her triumph, the neglected Eliza throws Higgins's slippers at him and tries to claw his face, and later returns his ring, which he throws into the fireplace. Her father, the dustman Alfred Doolittle, is made wealthy and miserable after Higgins jokingly calls him "the most original moralist in England" in a letter to an American millionaire, who leaves him a yearly grant to lecture for a moral reform society. The housekeeper Mrs. Pearce tells Higgins to stop swearing, and Higgins's former pupil Nepommuck appears at the ambassador's reception.

**Man and Superman**
Shaw's 1903 comedy of ideas about the "Life Force." The revolutionary John (Jack) Tanner, author of "The Revolutionist's Handbook" (published with the play), flees to Spain to escape the determined Ann Whitefield, who represents the Life Force; in the Sierra Nevada he is captured by the brigand leader Mendoza, a Jewish anarchist, but Ann finally wins him.

**"Don Juan in Hell"**
The long dream sequence in Act III of Man and Superman, often performed separately or cut from the play. Tanner becomes Don Juan, Ann becomes Doña Ana (who chooses to be twenty-seven years old in the afterlife), Roebuck Ramsden becomes the statue of the Commander, and Mendoza becomes the Devil, with whom Don Juan debates philosophy.

**Arms and the Man**
Shaw's 1894 comedy set during the Serbo-Bulgarian War of 1885, whose title comes from the first line of Virgil's Aeneid ("Arms and the man I sing"). The Swiss mercenary Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolates instead of ammunition, climbs into Raina Petkoff's bedroom window and is nicknamed the "chocolate-cream soldier"; Raina ends up engaged to him instead of the pompous hero Sergius. The servant Louka tells Nicola, who dreams of opening a shop in Sofia, "You have the soul of a servant," and he replies that is "the secret of success in service."

**Major Barbara**
Shaw's 1905 play in which Barbara Undershaft, a major in the Salvation Army, is disillusioned when the Army accepts donations from her father Andrew Undershaft, a munitions maker who calls poverty the worst of crimes, and from a whisky distiller. Undershaft, separated from his wife Lady Britomart, leaves his business to the foundling Greek scholar Adolphus Cusins, Barbara's fiancé, who translates Euripides with Barbara's name substituted for "loveliness." The bully Bill Walker hits the Salvation Army girl Jenny Hill on the mouth and later tries to make amends.

**Candida**
One of Shaw's "Plays Pleasant." Candida, wife of the Christian Socialist clergyman James Morell, must choose between him and the young poet Eugene Marchbanks, who loves her; she chooses her husband as "the weaker of the two." The play ends with the stage direction that the couple embrace but "they do not know the secret in the poet's heart."

**Mrs. Warren's Profession**
One of Shaw's "Plays Unpleasant," long banned by British censors. The educated Vivie Warren learns that her mother's fortune came from running a chain of brothels, a business in which Sir George Crofts is a partner; Praed is a friend of Mrs. Warren. Vivie rejects both her mother and her suitor Frank Gardner and ends the play working at Honoria Fraser's chambers.

**Heartbreak House**
Shaw's 1919 play, subtitled "A Fantasia in the Russian Manner on English Themes" (a nod to Chekhov). It is set at the house of the eccentric old inventor Captain Shotover, whose daughters are Hesione Hushabye and Lady Utterword; the play ends with an air raid in which bombs explode the dynamite Shotover has stored.

**Saint Joan**
Shaw's 1923 play about Joan of Arc, who has the Dauphin crowned Charles VII at Reims before she is tried and burned. The English chaplain de Stogumber is a fanatical supporter of her execution, and in the Epilogue, set 25 years after her death, Joan appears to Charles in a dream.

**Back to Methuselah**
Shaw's cycle of five plays on Creative Evolution. The first part, "In the Beginning," shows Adam and Eve in Eden realizing their own mortality after finding a fawn that has broken its neck, and the final part, "As Far as Thought Can Reach," is set in the year 31,920 AD.

**Caesar and Cleopatra, The Doctor's Dilemma, and other plays**
Caesar and Cleopatra has an "Alternative to the Prologue" in which the Egyptian guard captain Belzanor is warned of Caesar's invasion. In The Doctor's Dilemma, Sir Colenso Ridgeon must decide whether to save the talented but immoral painter Louis Dubedat with his new tuberculosis cure, and the play opens with his assistant Redpenny. Captain Brassbound's Conversion features Lady Cicely and Sir Howard, and You Never Can Tell, another "Play Pleasant," features the twins Philip and Dolly Clandon; Shaw also wrote The Devil's Disciple.

**The Fabian Society and The Perfect Wagnerite**
The Dublin-born Shaw began as a critic and was a leading member of the socialist Fabian Society. His book The Perfect Wagnerite interprets Wagner's Ring cycle as a socialist allegory about capitalism. He won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature.
